accessrestrict.head: Conditions Governing Access
accessrestrict.p: Open for research with select materials restricted as noted. Brittle or damaged items are available at the discretion of RAC. Researchers interested in accessing digital media (floppy disks, CDs, DVDs, etc.) or audiovisual material (audio cassettes, VHS, etc.) in this collection must use an access surrogate. The original items may not be accessed because of preservation concerns. To request an access surrogate be made, or if you are unsure if there is an access surrogate, please contact an archivist.

relatedmaterial.head: Stack File Index
relatedmaterial.p: The IHB Stack File Index is an obsolete dictionary card-catalog to the IHB's library. The index includes entries for author, title, subject, and place. Publications indexed here also appear in the IHB Stack Shelf-List. Each publication is indicated by an obsolete IHB library call number. Many of these publications are now found in the 'Rockefeller Foundation records, Pamphlet file (FA264)', however the publications are no longer filed by call number (although the old call numbers still appear on many of the volumes). Index cards filed under "Hookworm" have been separated from the Stack File Index's main A-Z arrangement, and placed into their own series: Stack File Index – 'Hookworm'.
The Stack File Index is located in drawers 51-55 of the 72 drawer cabinet next to the RAC's reading room.
An obsolete card "Stack Shelf-List", arranged by IHB library call-numbers, is located in drawers 49-50 of the 72-drawer cabinet next to the RAC's reading room.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Contains the correspondence and reports of the International Health Board/International Health Division (IHB/D) of the Rockefeller Foundation, including the Rockefeller Institute Virus Laboratories.

arrangement.head: Arrangement
arrangement.p: The International Health Board/Division records are arranged into five series:

userestrict.head: Conditions Governing Use
userestrict.p: Rockefeller Foundation has title, copyright, and literary rights in the collection, in so far as it holds them. Rockefeller Archive Center has authority to grant permission to cite and publish archival material from the collection.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents note
scopecontent.p: Subseries 1.1, Correspondence, General, is the administrative file of the International Health Commission and the International Health Board. It was collected in a central file, probably by a stenographer in charge of filing, Bertha Matson, who worked under Dr. J. A. Ferrell, the Assistant Director-General. In 1928, when the International Health Division superseded the Board, the Rockefeller Foundation also created a general correspondence file (Record Group 2). The Division's general correspondence is interfiled with that of the Foundation from 1928 through 1951, when the Division was disbanded.

The subseries consists mostly of letters to persons outside the organization or letters on subjects not directly related to specific projects. Occasional memoranda, reports and other material that is not strictly correspondence will be found in this subseries. Topics include insurance, leasing arrangements, customs clearance matters, exhibits, requests for information, meetings, subscriptions, reprints, invitations, declinations, itineraries, and routine correspondence with field staff on accounting and supply matters. Investigations in areas of possible project interest are included. Also included are letters that seem to belong in project files. Their presence can be credited to the field staff's tendency to cover several subjects in one letter and to the vagaries of the file clerk.

There are no complete files of administrative officers' correspondence collected as such. Their letters are dispersed throughout the files under the names of the addressees. However, a small amount of "personal" correspondence was kept for some officers, usually regarding some outside philanthropic interest. These folders will be found at the end of the year in which they were created, except for 1919 and 1920, which are in place alphabetically.

arrangement.head: Arrangement note
arrangement.p: The file is divided by year. Within each year, the arrangement is alphabetical by the name of the outside correspondent, then chronological under each name. Letters and replies are interfiled. Letters about a person may be filed under that person's name. Letters are also filed under names of institutions, companies or publications, as well as under some subject headings, such as "Equipment," "Leprosy" and "Mailing List." (The latter contains numerous changes of address for staff and fellows, plus some trip itineraries, and is useful in establishing the whereabouts of persons at particular times.)

Folder headings show alphabetical segments--"A-Ad", "Ae-Al," etc. Folders for individual correspondents are inserted when necessitated by volume; these follow the appropriate alphabetical segment. Letters and replies between two field staff members with individual folders are filed separately, not interfiled.

Documents were marked in red in the upper corner with the alphabetical letter under which they were to be filed; the determining name was also usually underlined in red. Later, the complete name was written in red in the upper right corner. In the case of company names or subject headings, occasional subheadings were used to indicate the writer, as in "Leprosy - Smith." Such letters would be arranged alphabetically by subheading within the "Leprosy" folder.

odd.head: IHB Correspondence Index
odd.p: A card index to 'Rockefeller Foundation records, Record Group 5: International Health Board/Division records, Series 1.1: Correspondence – General' and 'Series 1.2: Correspondence – Project' is available for researcher use.
'Series 1.1: Correspondence – General' files are indicated by the year, followed by the alphabetical arrangement of these files.
'Series 1.2: Correspondence – Project' files are indicated by the year, followed by an RF country code number.

The existence of material dated prior to 1917 is indicated on the cards by an ampersand (&). The index is not comprehensive. Some names that should have been indexed were not, and some indexed documents no longer exist. Some files were reclassified without revision of the index. This index is not included in the Rockefeller Foundation main index, but many entries in the RF main index are cross-referenced to the IHB index.

The filing and indexing system allowed considerable opportunity for interpretation. Cross-referencing was by no means exhaustive. To insure thorough research, it is wise to check all possible classifications for any particular document.
The IHB Correspondence Index is located in drawers 35-48 of the 72-drawer cabinet next to the RAC's reading room.

arrangement.head: Arrangement note
arrangement.p: These reports have been removed from a library classification and rearranged in the RF geographic number system. Reports that are international in scope are found in 100. Area numbers are used for reports covering several countries. Reports that cover several countries which are mentioned are filed with the first country named. Reports which are not international but so general as to be topical rather than geographic are found at the end of the subseries and filed geographically. The index to the stack material may still be used for locating material by author, title and subject.

Sometime prior to 1972, the photographs in the reports in this subseries were removed by Robert Clahn, preparatory to processing them for storage in the photograph collection. In some cases, he replaced the pages removed with photocopies of those pages, particularly where the pages included some text from the reports. The photographs were not processed, however, and remained in temporary storage until 1977.

In November, 1977, Steven Gelston and Warren Hovious completed the processing of these photos. They are now interfiled with other photos from the Rockefeller Foundation archives. The inventory for subseries 2, Special Reports, indicates where photos were removed from reports. The Processing Room copy of this inventory is now annotated to show the file classification number under which these photos will be found in the photo collection. The photos from any given report will be found together in one folder. The name of the report is the folder heading, and folder is also marked "RG 5, S 2."
Researchers using reports from which photos were removed should be given the corresponding photo folders along with the reports.

relatedmaterial.head: Field Staff Reports Index
relatedmaterial.p: The IHB's Field Staff Reports Index provides indexing to the Rockefeller Foundation records, Record Group 5: International Health Board/Division records, Series 3: Routine Reports is available for researcher use. The index cards are arranged A-Z by subject heading. Reports are indicated by year, then monthly in check-boxes.
The Field Staff Reports Index is located in drawer 33 of the 72-drawer cabinet next to the RAC's reading room.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents note
scopecontent.p: The Rockefeller Institute Virus Laboratories (RIVL) served as the base laboratory for the virus studies conducted by the Rockefeller Foundation's International Health Board/Division (IHB/D). Beginning in 1916, when William C. Gorgas' special commission visited South America, the IHB/D supported field research as part of its international campaign against yellow fever. By the late 1920's, the difficulty and expense of conducting field research in Brazil and West Africa made apparent the need for a central lab for the completion of promising viral investigations developed in those primitive settings. At the urging of Frederick F. Russell, IHD director, such a lab was established in 1929. Headed by Wilbur A. Sawyer, the lab rented space at The Rockefeller Institute for Medical Research in New York City.

In its early years the RIVL was devoted primarily to yellow fever research, resulting in the 1935 development of the vaccine 17D by Dr. Max Theiler. As yellow fever research became increasingly successful, other viral diseases drew the attention of the IHD scientists. By 1944, as World War II presented the prospect of mass epidemics, attention was focused on twelve specific diseases. Most notable among these were influenza, malaria, typhus and yellow fever. The final stage of RIVL research, begun in 1949, was the collection and classification of arboviruses (viruses carried by insects). Again, field labs were established around the world with the New York lab serving as the central clearinghouse. In December of 1964 the New York lab was incorporated into the Yale School of Medicine, becoming the Yale Arbovirus Research Unit.

The title of this subseries may be misleading. It documents not just the work of the Rockefeller Institute Virus Lab but the activities of the IHB/D scientists in the field. The RIVL records reflect the role of the New York lab as the base lab and reveal the informal information network used by the IHB/D scientists to keep one another informed. Instead of preparing systematic reports, the scientists wrote lengthy, detailed letters to exchange opinions and to describe their work, travels and personnel matters. The research most frequently discussed concerns the epidemiology, diagnosis and control of influenza, malaria, typhus and yellow fever.

There is also extensive correspondence on routine matters such as the ordering of supplies, equipment and animal stock; travel itineraries; and manuscript critiques. Collaborations with chemical and pharmaceutical firms and government agencies also are documented. There is some administrative material but very little revealing the organizational structure or administration of the New York or other labs, their role within the IHB/D, or the overall administration of the IHB/D.

Research in the RIVL records requires creativity as well as familiarity with the topic on the part of the researcher. Material on any given person or subject can be found in several different files. For example, to locate material on a particular scientist the research should look at that scientist's file and also at the files of those individuals with whom the scientist was likely to have corresponded.

The RIVL records are international in scope with a concentration on Latin America, Africa and the U.S. The files are in alphabetical order with a chronological arrangement within each folder. The earliest records are equipment lists from 1915 but the bulk of the material covers the mid-1920s through 1949.

arrangement.head: Arrangement note
arrangement.p: The files are in alphabetical order with a chronological arrangement within each folder.
